title: Delaware City refinery launches public air-monitoring website during equipment repairs
description: Five fence-line monitoring stations will track sulfur dioxide and other emissions in real time as refinery undergoes four weeks of maintenance DELAWARE CITY — Delaware City Refining Company has launched a new public-facing air quality monitoring website as the refinery begins equipment repairs expected to temporarily increase emissions during a planned maint[...]
text:
Photo: Delaware City, Courtesy Kayak.com.


Five fence-line monitoring stations will track sulfur dioxide and other emissions in real time as refinery undergoes four weeks of maintenance


DELAWARE CITY — Delaware City Refining Company has launched a new public-facing air quality monitoring website as the refinery begins equipment repairs expected to temporarily increase emissions during a planned maintenance period.


The website, delcity-air.com, allows residents, community members and other interested parties to monitor real-time air quality data collected from five fence-line monitoring stations positioned around and near the refinery property.


The monitoring system continuously measures air quality conditions around the facility perimeter and nearby communities, reporting data in both 5-minute and 1-hour averages to provide detailed and timely visibility into conditions at and around the refinery.

Five monitoring stations are positioned around the refinery

The launch comes as DCRC prepares to repair its coker carbon monoxide boiler after operators detected signs of a possible water-tube leak. The company said the repair work will require a temporary shutdown of the boiler and the diversion of flue gas through an alternative emissions control device.


The repairs are expected to take approximately four weeks.


Company officials said the monitoring system was installed to comply with Delaware Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control requirements for volatile organic compound monitoring, but the refinery voluntarily expanded the system to include sulfur dioxide monitoring as well.


The addition of sulfur dioxide monitoring is significant because sulfur dioxide is one of the primary emissions expected to increase during the maintenance period.


According to DCRC, the fence-line monitoring network is designed to provide “comprehensive coverage” of both the refinery perimeter and adjacent neighborhoods. The stations continuously transmit data to the public website, where registered users can view current readings and subscribe to customized alerts.

Public access and real-time alerts

The company’s Health, Safety and Environmental team said air-quality professionals will review the monitoring data daily to verify accuracy, ensure regulatory compliance and respond to any operational concerns.


DCRC said it also plans to work closely with DNREC throughout the repair process, comparing company monitoring information with state air-monitoring results.


The public website represents one of the more visible transparency efforts surrounding refinery operations in Delaware in recent years, giving residents near the industrial complex near Delaware City direct access to live environmental monitoring information.

Transparency effort follows years of scrutiny

The Delaware City refinery has long been one of the state’s most closely watched industrial facilities because of its size, emissions profile and proximity to surrounding communities along the Delaware River corridor.


The new monitoring system and public website are intended to provide residents with more immediate access to environmental information during both routine operations and maintenance events while also giving regulators and the public additional tools to evaluate air-quality conditions in real time.

title: Voter Turnout Shapes Key Delaware School Board Races as Challengers Score Major Wins
description: Red Clay and Appoquinimink voters deliver sweeping changes while Milford backs stability WILMINGTON — Delaware voters delivered several high-profile school board shakeups Tuesday night, signaling strong public engagement in races that often draw little attention but carry significant influence over local education policy, budgets, and district leadership. Th[...]
text:
School board elections in Delaware historically attract low turnout, often in the single digits, but this year’s contests drew heightened attention amid statewide conversations about academic performance, school safety, district spending, and controversial school restructuring plans.
Red Clay and Appoquinimink voters deliver sweeping changes while Milford backs stability
WILMINGTON — Delaware voters delivered several high-profile school board shakeups Tuesday night, signaling strong public engagement in races that often draw little attention but carry significant influence over local education policy, budgets, and district leadership.
The biggest headlines came from the Red Clay and Appoquinimink school districts, where challengers defeated sitting board presidents in races shaped by debates over transparency, school direction, and public trust. In Milford, meanwhile, voters overwhelmingly backed experience and continuity.
The results underscored a broader theme emerging across Delaware: democracy works when voters participate.
School board elections in Delaware historically attract low turnout, often in the single digits, but this year’s contests drew heightened attention amid statewide conversations about academic performance, school safety, district spending, and controversial school restructuring plans.
Julia Keleher, executive director of First State Educate, said the elections reinforced the idea that sustained public participation is essential to improving schools and shaping district priorities.  First State Educate and Citizens for Delaware Schools both published voter guides and helpful information to assist residents in making their decisions.
“Participation is the key to getting better results from our schools and establishing the right direction and priorities for students and families,” Keleher said. “Last night showed that participation is the key to positive change.”
Nancy Mercante, executive director of Citizens for Delaware Schools, said Tuesday’s results reflected growing public demand for stronger community engagement from school leaders. “Candidates and elected officials need to listen to voters and parents,” Mercante said. “Tonight’s results demonstrated that involving the community and engaging parents matters.”
Red Clay voters replace board president
In the closely watched Red Clay Consolidated School District race, challenger Jenny Howard defeated incumbent board president Vic Leonard by more than 300 votes in District C.
Howard received 1,095 votes to Leonard’s 726, according to unofficial Delaware Department of Elections totals. More than 1,800 ballots were cast in the race.
Howard posted especially strong numbers at Dickinson High School, Hockessin PAL, Marbrook Elementary and McKean High School polling locations. Leonard performed best at A.I. du Pont High School and remained competitive at Joseph E. Johnson School and North Star Elementary.
The race became one of Delaware’s most closely watched school board contests following months of debate surrounding Red Clay’s proposed “reimagining” of McKean High School and concerns about transparency in district planning.
Howard had campaigned heavily on community engagement, clearer communication and slowing major district decisions until more public input could be gathered.
Leonard, who had served as board president during several contentious district discussions, defended the district’s long-term planning efforts and emphasized the need to address enrollment challenges and aging facilities.
Following the victory, Howard thanked voters for participating in the democratic process and said the election demonstrated the importance of community involvement in local schools.
“I’m grateful to everyone who came out to vote, shared their opinions and participated in this election,” Howard said. “No matter who people supported, this level of engagement matters because our schools belong to the community. I’m looking forward to getting started and working together with the other board members on behalf of students and families across Red Clay.”
The outcome represents a significant leadership shift for one of Delaware’s largest school districts.
Appoquinimink voters send message for change
The Appoquinimink School District election also produced a dramatic shakeup, with voters removing two incumbents, including board president Richard Forsten.
Britney Mumford led all candidates with 2,123 votes, while Elena Brenner secured the second winning spot with 1,955 votes.
Incumbent Nichelle DeWitt finished fourth with 787 votes, while Forsten placed fifth with 362 votes.
Candidate Mark E. Heck finished third with 1,752 votes, narrowly missing election.
The scale of the results reflected a broad voter movement rather than a narrow upset. Mumford and Brenner posted strong performances throughout the district, including major wins at Cedar Lane Elementary, Middletown High School, Old State Elementary and Townsend Elementary.
The Appoquinimink races unfolded during a period of rapid district growth and increasing public debate over development, classroom capacity, district spending and governance.
The election outcome suggests many voters were looking for new voices and a more direct connection between district leadership and parents.
Milford voters favor continuity
While Red Clay and Appoquinimink voters embraced change, Milford School District voters strongly supported incumbent Cindy McKenzie in the District C race.
McKenzie defeated challenger Nik Dutta-Roy by a commanding 378-36 margin.
A longtime educator and former Milford principal, McKenzie campaigned on her decades of experience within the district and her understanding of Milford’s schools and families.
The overwhelming margin suggested broad voter confidence in existing district leadership and stability.
School boards carry major influence
Though often overshadowed by statewide elections, school boards control multi-million-dollar budgets, oversee district leadership, shape curriculum priorities and make decisions affecting thousands of students and families.
This year’s elections arrived during a period of elevated public attention on education issues across Delaware, including student achievement, district finances, school safety and long-term planning.
In addition to the marquee races in Red Clay, Appoquinimink and Milford, voters across the state also selected school board members in Christina, Colonial, Caesar Rodney and Delmar.
Among other winners Tuesday night:
• Celita Cherry retained her seat in Christina School District.• Dawn Green and Carlos Dispres won in Colonial School District races.• Incumbents David Failing and Mike Morasco prevailed in Caesar Rodney.• Neal Baker and Jordan Johnson captured seats in Delmar.
Final certified results are expected from the Delaware Department of Elections in the coming days.

title: What Lil Nas X has to do with a debate over CA mental health law
description: In the battle over whether to change a California crime law, both supporters and critics are waging their campaign not only through crime statistics but also by invoking harrowing anecdotes — including one involving American rapper Lil Nas X. As Gagandeep Singh for CalMatters explains, legislators are advancing a bill that would lower the threshold […]
text:
Lil Nas X, whose legal name is Montero Lamar Hill, appears in court in Los Angeles on March 12, 2026. Photo by Daniel Cole/Pool via AP




In the battle over whether to change a California crime law, both supporters and critics are waging their campaign not only through crime statistics but also by invoking harrowing anecdotes — including one involving American rapper Lil Nas X.
As Gagandeep Singh for CalMatters explains, legislators are advancing a bill that would lower the threshold a judge could use to deny mental health diversion for people accused of certain crimes. 
The bill would tweak a 2018 law that currently allows judges to block diversion if they find the defendant poses “an unreasonable risk of danger to public safety.” But by changing the standard to “a substantial and undue risk,” which the bill proposes, it would make it easier for judges to reject diversion and send defendants to prison instead.
Proponents, which include police unions and law enforcement leaders, argue that it closes a loophole that allows violent offenders to walk free. In his support of the measure, Sacramento County District Attorney Thien Ho cites multiple cases from Sacramento County in which suspects committed serious offenses after being granted diversion.
The most recent case occurred last year, when deputies arrested 40-year-old Jordon Murray for allegedly stabbing another person to death in Fair Oaks. Murray was previously released from jail under a mental health diversion.
But public defenders and civil liberties organizations say the 2018 law is working as intended, and that judges already wield enough power to limit access to diversion. In illustrating the success of diversion, the California Public Defenders Association points to Lil Nas X, a prominent music artist whose real name is Montero Lamar Hill.
In 2025 police found Hill, nearly naked, wandering the streets of Los Angeles. Officers said Hill charged at them, and he faced four felony counts and up to five years in prison. A judge granted him diversion, saying at the time, “When treated, he is much better off and society is much better off.”

Kate Chatfield, executive director of the association, in an April press release: “Diversion is not a loophole. … It is a promise that the system will respond to human beings as human beings, that treatment is possible, that a crisis does not have to define a life.” 

The Senate’s Appropriations Committee will decide on Thursday whether the bill moves forward.
Read more.



The issues defining California’s future don’t wait, and neither should you. From AI to immigration to the next governor’s challenges, join CalMatters on May 21 for the Ideas Festival and be part of the conversation. Secure your seat.
We’re bringing our voter guide to life through VotingMatters events across California this month, in collaboration with on-the-ground partners: Local news organizations, colleges, libraries, churches and nonprofit organizations. Our next events are tonight in Los Angeles and Thursday evening in Bakersfield. Plus, we have a DIY kit to host your own event. 
Focus on Inland Empire: Each Wednesday, CalMatters Inland Empire reporter Aidan McGloin surveys the big stories from that part of California. Read his newsletter and sign up here to receive it.

Other Stories You Should Know


‘Borrowed time’ on gas supply


Gas prices on display at a filling station in Bakersfield on April 15, 2026. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters




If your wallet is already hurting at the pump, things may get even worse in the next few weeks, reports CalMatters’ Alejandro Lazo.
At a recent legislative oversight hearing, Siva Gunda, the vice chairperson of the California Energy Commission, said the state’s fuel supplies look stable for the next six weeks. After about mid-June, however, it’ll cost California — and consumers, in turn — a lot more money to secure more oil and gas.
As of this week, Californians pay an average of $6.15 a gallon — the highest in the country. But if the conflict in Iran drags on, the average in California would likely settle “under seven, more like $6.50,” Gunda said.
Severin Borenstein, a UC Berkeley energy economist who was also at the hearing, has a more pessimistic view: If the Strait of Hormuz stays closed another 60 days, the price of crude could increase by another $40 to $80 a barrel, he said. Each $40 increase adds about another $1 per gallon at the pump.

Borenstein: “I know we all hope that doesn’t happen and that the flow of oil resumes, but the reality is we are on borrowed time as we run down inventories.”

Read more.



1 million students affected by Canvas hack


A laptop displays a maintenance screen as a user tries to log into Canvas at their home in Stockton on May 7, 2026. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters




As California schools assess the fallout from the major Canvas cyberattack, at least one state lawmaker wants answers.
Teachers use the popular academic software Canvas to give tests, communicate with students, post grades and more. Last week a hacker group claimed to obtain sensitive data through Canvas and demanded a ransom. 
Canvas’ outage hit California especially hard — likely affecting more than 1 million of the state’s university students, write CalMatters’ Colin Lecher and Mikhail Zinshteyn. The hack has raised serious questions about whether schools should be so dependent on centralized solutions for their online education tools. Though these services enable schools to easily manage everything on a single platform, a security breach of one company also leaves vulnerable the data of numerous institutions.
The outage prompted Sen. Melissa Hurtado to seek a legislative audit into California’s heavy reliance on Canvas. 

Hurtado, a Bakersfield Democrat: The “breach exposes the growing risks of concentrating massive amounts of student records … into a single platform.”

Read more.



And lastly: New bill tackles CA’s public defender crisis


The courtroom in Department 20 at the Placer County Superior Court in Roseville on Jan. 23, 2026. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




Following a 2025 investigative series by CalMatters’ Anat Rubin that exposed the systemic failures of California’s public defender system, lawmakers introduced a bill that would require counties to report basic information about their public defender services, such as how many cases attorneys handle. Read more.






California Voices

CalMatters contributor Robert Greene: For Los Angelenos of a certain age, the governor’s race may come as a surprise for voters who remember the 2001 mayoral race — when the clean-cut Xavier Becerra and the electric Antonio Villaraigosa first squared off.

title: It’s not (just) location: Why gas is so high in NV even though US is a net exporter of oil products
description: Regular unleaded gasoline was 29% higher in the U.S. in April than it was in April 2025, according to consumer price index (CPI) data — the inflation report — released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics Tuesday. Relatedly, airline fares are 21% higher than they were a year ago, an increase driven primarily by the […]
text:
(Photo: Hugh Jackson/Nevada Current)Regular unleaded gasoline was 29% higher in the U.S. in April than it was in April 2025, according to consumer price index (CPI) data — the inflation report — released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics Tuesday.
Relatedly, airline fares are 21% higher than they were a year ago, an increase driven primarily by the cost of jet fuel, according to the CPI report.
The U.S. exports more petroleum products than it imports. Thanks in part to that domestic production buffer, the impact of the Iran war on fuel prices is not nearly as painful in the U.S. as it is in African, Asian, and European nations.
But it is still deeply troubling for U.S. households, especially in Nevadan and other Western states which are captive to the California gasoline market.
The overwhelming majority of gasoline purchased in Nevada is refined in California. Critics in both states argue California’s environmental regulation of both the oil industry and auto emissions make refining more costly, which in turn has been blamed for refineries closing in California.
Since sufficient infrastructure for alternative supplies was never developed, Nevada remains bound to the California market, and Nevadans typically pay about 20% more for gas than the national average.
The U.S. is a net exporter of petroleum products primarily because it exports a tremendous amount of liquefied natural gas.
But the U.S. is still a net importer of crude oil.
Nevada Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo is among those who have suggested California environmental policies are as much if not more to blame than Trump’s war in Iran for spiking gasoline prices in Nevada.
Last year, 23% of the oil refined in California was drilled in California, according to the California Energy Commission. Another 16% came from Alaska. The rest came from Canada, South America, Guyana, and the Persian Gulf states of Iraq, Saudi Arabia, and United Arab Emirates. 
The Gulf states together accounted for nearly a third of oil refined in California in 2025.
Refineries throughout the U.S. also rely on imported crude, at least partially, to use to blend with domestic oil while making assorted products (regular gas, diesel, jet fuel, etc.). 
When U.S. refiners import crude oil from other nations, they are competing with purchasers the world over, and have to pay a price that is being set by the international market.
As it was in the 20th century, the U.S. oil (and gasoline) market remains intertwined with and reliant on global oil shipments. That’s why the average price of gas in Nevada, according to AAA, is about $1.20 per gallon higher than it was a year ago, and why gas prices are higher not just in Nevada, but around the nation and the world.
At least two fuel companies are exploring pipeline expansions that would help Nevada wean itself from such heavy reliance on the California gas market. That effort is lauded by state officials from the standpoint of reliability, and also as potential means to put Nevada’s gas prices a little more in line with national averages.
Meanwhile, unleaded gas and jet fuel weren’t the only costs to see substantial increases in the most recent CPI report.
Coffee was 18% more expensive last month than in April 2025. Other items with year-over-year double-digit percentage increases include video streaming service (17%), steak (16%), jewelry (16%), computer software and accessories (14%), and fresh vegetables (11.5%), the latter largely driven by the whopping increase in the price of tomatoes (39.7%).
Like many other items, from car parts to dishes, the tomatoes especially reflect higher diesel (transportation) costs combined with another inflationary consequence of U.S. policy: tariffs.
